title: Class 5 Maths Smart Charts (NCERT Chapter 12) Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Smart Charts (NCERT Ch 12) + Quiz
meta_desc: Class 5 Maths Smart Charts made easy: tally marks, tables, pictographs and bar graphs from NCERT Chapter 12, with worked case studies and a free quiz.
excerpt: Tally marks, tables, pictographs, bar graphs — NCERT Class 5 Chapter 12 is really about one skill: turning a messy pile of data into a chart that answers a question. Here is how to read it, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A Class 5 child counts the vehicles passing the school gate for ten minutes and comes back with a page that reads ‘car, car, bike, auto, car, bus, bike, car…’ — forty scribbled words and no way to answer the one question the teacher actually asked: which vehicle is most common? That gap, between raw data and a clear answer, is exactly what Class 5 Maths Smart Charts (NCERT Chapter 12) is about. The chapter teaches four tools — tally marks, tables, pictographs and bar graphs — and, more importantly, when to reach for each one.

I have taught this chapter enough times to know where ten-year-olds trip up. It is almost never the drawing. It is the reading — pulling the right number off a chart and comparing two bars without recounting from scratch. So this guide spends most of its time on that, with two solved case studies of the kind you meet in the exam.

What NCERT Chapter 12 actually covers

Strip away the pictures and Smart Charts asks a child to do three things in order: collect data, organise it, and then represent it so a question becomes easy to answer. The four representations build on each other.

  • Tally marks — the fast way to count things as they happen. Four upright strokes, then a fifth stroke drawn across the group to bundle it into a five.
  • Frequency table — the tally turned into neat numbers, one row per category. This is the bridge to every chart that follows.
  • Pictograph — a picture chart where one symbol stands for a fixed number (the key), so a half symbol means half of that.
  • Bar graph — bars whose heights are read off a numbered scale. Best when you want to compare quantities at a glance.

Tally marks: counting without losing your place

Tally marks solve a real problem — you cannot count moving things and write full numbers at the same time. The rule Class 5 must lock in is the bundle of five: draw four vertical strokes, then strike the fifth diagonally across them. A group like this is read instantly as 5, so 5 and 5 and 2 leftover strokes is 12 without any recounting.

Here is a tally becoming a frequency table for that vehicle survey:

VehicleTallyFrequency
Car|||| |||| ||12
Bike|||| |||8
Auto||||5
Bus|||3

Once the frequency column exists, the answers fall out: most common vehicle is the car (12), least common is the bus (3), and 28 vehicles passed in all. Notice we never went back to the original scribbles.

Pictographs: the picture is only as good as its key

A pictograph draws each category as repeated symbols. The single most important part is the key — the note that says, for example, one book symbol equals 10 books. Miss the key and every reading is wrong.

The classic exam twist is the half symbol. If one symbol equals 10 and a row shows three-and-a-half symbols, that is 3 × 10 + 5 = 35. Children who have only ever seen whole symbols freeze here, so it is worth practising deliberately.

Case study 1: the class library

A Class 5 library records how many books were borrowed in a week. One book symbol on their pictograph stands for 10 books. Maths shows 4 symbols, Science shows 3 symbols, Story books show 5 and a half symbols, and Poetry shows 1 symbol.

  • Story books borrowed: 5 × 10 + 5 = 55 — the most popular.
  • Maths books borrowed: 4 × 10 = 40.
  • Poetry borrowed: 1 × 10 = 10 — the least.
  • Story books minus Science: 55 − 30 = 25 more.

Bar graphs: reading heights off a scale

Bar graphs are the tool for comparison. The height of each bar sits against a numbered axis, and the scale — whether each line is worth 1, 2, 5 or 10 — decides every value. The most common Class 5 error is counting grid lines instead of reading the numbers, so on a scale marked in tens a bar reaching the fourth line is read as 4 rather than 40.

Case study 2: favourite fruits in Class 5B

A survey of Class 5B is drawn as a bar graph with the scale going up in 2s. The bars read: Mango 10, Banana 6, Apple 8, Orange 4, Grapes 2.

  • Total children surveyed: 10 + 6 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 30.
  • Favourite fruit: Mango (tallest bar, 10 votes).
  • Mango more than Orange: 10 − 4 = 6 children.
  • Fruits chosen by more than 5 children: Mango, Banana and Apple — three fruits.

Choosing the right chart for the question

This is the skill the exam quietly rewards, and the one the chapter title hints at — being smart about which chart you pick. Use a tally while you are still counting. Use a pictograph when the numbers are tidy multiples and you want something friendly to look at. Use a bar graph when the whole point is to compare who has more. If a question asks ‘how many more’ or ‘which is greatest’, a bar graph almost always answers it fastest.

You want to…Best chartWhy
Count things as they happenTally marksNo writing numbers mid-count
Store the counts neatlyFrequency tableOne clear number per row
Show tidy round numbers nicelyPictographSymbols with a key are easy to read
Compare quantitiesBar graphHeights compare at a glance

One honest caveat before the quiz

Do not let a child rush to draw a beautiful chart before checking the totals add up. In my experience the marks are lost not in the artwork but in a careless subtraction or a misread key. Slow down on the reading; the drawing is the easy part.

Try the quiz, then the case-study workbook

The eight-question quiz below covers tally marks, tables, pictographs and bar graphs at exactly Class 5 level — let your child attempt it and read the explanations for anything missed. When they are ready for full exam-style practice, the printable case-study workbook at the end walks through survey passages with complete step-by-step solutions.

quiz.title: Class 5 Smart Charts Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on tally marks, tables, pictographs and bar graphs from NCERT Chapter 12. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How is the number 5 shown in tally marks?
options: Four strokes with a fifth struck across them
questions.explanation: In tally marks, four upright strokes are bundled by a fifth stroke drawn diagonally across them, so one bundle reads as 5.

questions.q: A frequency table shows Car 12, Bike 8, Auto 5, Bus 3. How many vehicles in all?
In a pictograph, one book symbol stands for 10 books. What do 3 and a half symbols mean?
questions.explanation: 3 whole symbols are 30, and half a symbol is 5, so the total is 30 + 5 = 35 books.

questions.q: Why must every pictograph have a key?
options: To tell you how many one symbol stands for
questions.explanation: The key tells you the value of one symbol. Without it you cannot know whether a symbol means 1, 5 or 10.

questions.q: On a bar graph the scale goes up in 10s and a bar reaches the 4th line. What value is it?
questions.explanation: Read the scale, not the lines. Each line is worth 10, so the 4th line is 4 x 10 = 40.

questions.q: Which chart is best when you want to compare which quantity is the greatest?
questions.explanation: A bar graph lets you compare heights at a glance, so the tallest bar is the greatest quantity.

questions.q: In Class 5B: Mango 10, Banana 6, Apple 8, Orange 4. How many more chose Mango than Orange?
questions.explanation: Subtract: 10 minus 4 = 6 more children chose Mango than Orange.

questions.q: A tally shows one bundle of five and three more strokes. What number is it?
questions.explanation: One bundle is 5 and three leftover strokes add 3, so 5 + 3 = 8.

faq.q: What is Smart Charts in Class 5 Maths?
faq.a: Smart Charts is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 12. It teaches data handling — collecting data and organising it using tally marks, frequency tables, pictographs and bar graphs so a question can be answered quickly.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pictograph and a bar graph?
faq.a: A pictograph uses repeated symbols with a key, where one symbol stands for a fixed number. A bar graph uses bars whose heights are read against a numbered scale. Bar graphs are usually better for comparing quantities.

faq.q: How do you read a half symbol in a pictograph?
faq.a: Check the key first. If one symbol equals 10, then half a symbol equals 5. So three and a half symbols mean 3 × 10 + 5 = 35.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in bar graph questions?
faq.a: Counting grid lines instead of reading the scale. If each line is worth 10, a bar at the third line is 30, not 3. Always read the numbers marked on the axis.
